title: Fargo Rating Explained: What Your Pool Skill Number Really Means
description: What is a Fargo Rating? A plain-English guide to the pool skill number, what 300, 500 and 700 mean, and how handicaps keep matches fair.
body:
"What's your Fargo?" It is one of the most common questions at a tournament desk, and if you are new to pool it can sound like a secret code. Good news: it is just a number, and once you understand it, you will know how you stack up, how to find fair opponents and why handicapped matches can be so much fun.

What is a Fargo Rating?

A Fargo Rating is a skill number for pocket billiards players, covering 8-ball, 9-ball and 10-ball. FargoRate says it computes ratings for amateur and professional players around the world on one uniform scale, so a player in a small-town league and a touring pro can be compared with the same yardstick.

The idea is borrowed from rating systems like the one used in chess: your results against opponents of known ratings move your number up or down.

How does the number work?

The scale has no official top or bottom, but there are handy landmarks. According to FargoRate, about two-thirds of established ratings land between 370 and 590, and about 95% fall between 260 and 690. Professionals generally rate above 700, and the elite are above 800.

Dr. Dave, a well-known pool instructor and writer, offers a friendly rough guide:

  • 200: a beginner who has probably never run a table
  • 300: common for casual, non-competitive league players
  • 400: can occasionally run out the first time at the table
  • 500: a good local league player
  • 600: has strung together three-in-a-row runs multiple times
  • 700 to 800: top players and world-class professionals

Treat these as signposts, not strict labels. Everyone has off days, and a 500 who is hot can beat a 550.

What does a gap between two players mean?

This is the clever part. The gap between two ratings predicts how many games each player should win. FargoRate explains that a 100-point gap is roughly a 1:2 game-win ratio, 200 points is about 1:4, and 300 points is about 1:8.

In plain words: if you are 100 points below your opponent, you should win about one game for every two they win. That is why a race to seven between a 500 and a 600 is not a coin flip, but it is also far from hopeless for the lower-rated player.

Why handicaps make matches fairer

Because the gap predicts results, tournaments and leagues can use it to even things out. The lower-rated player gets a head start, such as needing fewer games to win the match. Organizers set the exact spots, and they differ from event to event, so always check the tournament flyer or ask the director. Our guide on reading a tournament flyer shows where those details usually hide.

The result is a match where both players have a real chance, which means more close, exciting finishes and fewer lopsided afternoons. If you are nervous about your first event, a handicapped tournament is a wonderful place to start. Our first pool tournament guide walks through what to expect.

How do you get a rating?

Ratings come from games you play against rated opponents. FargoRate says league play enters through its league software and tournament play through CueMatch or other tournament tools, and there is an app for Apple and Android phones. A rating based on 200 or more games is considered "established." Before that, it is a good estimate that keeps improving as you play.

No rating yet? Do not worry. Many players first meet the system by simply joining a league or entering a tournament that reports results. If you want to find one, our pool league guide explains the main options, and the pool hall directory helps you find a place to play near you.

How to use your number the smart way

  • Track progress, not pride. Watching your rating creep up over a few months is a great motivator.
  • Pick fair matches. Playing people a little above you is the fastest way to learn.
  • Remember it is only an estimate. The number is a prediction based on past games, not a verdict on how much you enjoy the game.
  • Practice with purpose. Pair the number with a few solo drills and you will see it move.

Watching the pros with fresh eyes

With the Mosconi Cup in Orlando set for Nov 27-30, you will hear commentators talk about how hard the best players are to beat. Now you know why: pros sit up around 800, where a 100-point gap in either direction changes the odds dramatically. Check what is on in the coming days on our this weekend page and enjoy the matches.

The bottom line

A Fargo Rating is a simple, friendly way to describe pool skill. Know your number, play fair matches, and have fun climbing, one rack at a time. So, do you know your Fargo yet?
